cards.explanation: The rest of the chromosome may retain its usual copy number.
cards.text: Loss of one copy of a segment in a diploid cell creates {{c1::partial monosomy}} for that region.
cards.question: Loss of one copy of a segment in a diploid cell creates {{c1::partial monosomy}} for that region.

cards.explanation: Terminal segments are often lost before the ends fuse.
cards.text: If both broken ends of one chromosome join to each other, the result is a {{c1::ring chromosome}}.
cards.question: If both broken ends of one chromosome join to each other, the result is a {{c1::ring chromosome}}.

cards.explanation: The two flanking ends rejoin. A terminal deletion instead removes the end of a chromosome.
cards.text: An internal chromosome segment is lost after two breaks in an {{c1::interstitial deletion}}.
cards.question: An internal chromosome segment is lost after two breaks in an {{c1::interstitial deletion}}.

cards.explanation: An internal deletion leaves material on both sides of the missing segment.
cards.text: A deletion extending from a breakpoint to the tip of a chromosome is {{c1::terminal}}.
cards.question: A deletion extending from a breakpoint to the tip of a chromosome is {{c1::terminal}}.

cards.explanation: It cannot attach normally to the spindle and may be lost.
cards.text: A fragment lacking a {{c1::centromere}} generally fails to segregate reliably during cell division.
cards.question: A fragment lacking a {{c1::centromere}} generally fails to segregate reliably during cell division.

cards.explanation: The allele is expressed because there is no functional copy opposite it.
cards.text: When a deletion unmasks a recessive allele on the remaining homologue, the inheritance pattern is called {{c1::pseudodominance}}.
cards.question: When a deletion unmasks a recessive allele on the remaining homologue, the inheritance pattern is called {{c1::pseudodominance}}.

cards.explanation: This differs from a deletion exposing a recessive pathogenic variant on the other homologue.
cards.text: Loss of one allele causes disease through {{c1::haploinsufficiency}} when the remaining normal copy makes too little product.
cards.question: Loss of one allele causes disease through {{c1::haploinsufficiency}} when the remaining normal copy makes too little product.

cards.explanation: The cry is a clue to the underlying 5p deletion.
cards.text: The high-pitched cry in cri-du-chat syndrome is associated with abnormal development of the {{c1::larynx}}.
cards.question: The high-pitched cry in cri-du-chat syndrome is associated with abnormal development of the {{c1::larynx}}.

cards.explanation: The p arm is the short arm. The child can still have 46 chromosomes.
cards.text: A characteristic high-pitched cry in an infant with a deletion of {{c1::5p}} suggests cri-du-chat syndrome.
cards.question: A characteristic high-pitched cry in an infant with a deletion of {{c1::5p}} suggests cri-du-chat syndrome.

cards.explanation: It is one of the findings associated with a 5p deletion.
cards.text: A small head circumference relative to age and sex is called {{c1::microcephaly}}.
cards.question: A small head circumference relative to age and sex is called {{c1::microcephaly}}.

cards.explanation: Counting chromosomes alone does not detect the missing segment.
cards.text: A child with a 5p deletion can have a chromosome count of {{c1::46}}.
cards.question: A child with a 5p deletion can have a chromosome count of {{c1::46}}.

cards.explanation: Epigenetic marks can silence one parental copy in particular tissues.
cards.text: Parent-of-origin-dependent expression of an allele is called genomic {{c1::imprinting}}.
cards.question: Parent-of-origin-dependent expression of an allele is called genomic {{c1::imprinting}}.

cards.explanation: The mark carries information about parental origin.
cards.text: Imprinting can change gene expression without changing the DNA {{c1::sequence}}.
cards.question: Imprinting can change gene expression without changing the DNA {{c1::sequence}}.

cards.explanation: The new marks correspond to the sex of the individual producing the gametes.
cards.text: During gamete formation, parental imprinting marks are erased and {{c1::re-established}}.
cards.question: During gamete formation, parental imprinting marks are erased and {{c1::re-established}}.

cards.explanation: The clinical pattern points towards loss of maternal neuronal UBE3A expression.
cards.text: Severe speech impairment, developmental delay and frequent laughter suggest {{c1::Angelman syndrome}} in the chromosome 15 example.
cards.question: Severe speech impairment, developmental delay and frequent laughter suggest {{c1::Angelman syndrome}} in the chromosome 15 example.

cards.explanation: The paternal allele is normally silenced in many neurons.
cards.text: Loss of expression of the maternal neuronal {{c1::UBE3A}} allele causes Angelman syndrome.
cards.question: Loss of expression of the maternal neuronal {{c1::UBE3A}} allele causes Angelman syndrome.

cards.explanation: A paternal deletion is one cause. The same chromosome region has different effects according to parental origin.
cards.text: Prader–Willi syndrome results from loss of expression of normally active {{c1::paternal}} genes in 15q11–q13.
cards.question: Prader–Willi syndrome results from loss of expression of normally active {{c1::paternal}} genes in 15q11–q13.

cards.explanation: Loss of the paternal contribution and loss of maternal UBE3A expression have different consequences.
cards.text: For a deletion involving the imprinted 15q11–q13 region, the syndrome depends on the {{c1::parent of origin}}.
cards.question: For a deletion involving the imprinted 15q11–q13 region, the syndrome depends on the {{c1::parent of origin}}.

cards.explanation: Feeding difficulty in infancy can precede excessive appetite in childhood.
cards.text: In a newborn with Prader–Willi syndrome, poor feeding often reflects hypotonia and a weak {{c1::suck}}.
cards.question: In a newborn with Prader–Willi syndrome, poor feeding often reflects hypotonia and a weak {{c1::suck}}.

cards.explanation: Persistent hunger contributes to rapid weight gain in childhood.
cards.text: After poor feeding and hypotonia in infancy, Prader–Willi syndrome commonly features {{c1::hyperphagia}}.
cards.question: After poor feeding and hypotonia in infancy, Prader–Willi syndrome commonly features {{c1::hyperphagia}}.

cards.explanation: One recombinant chromosome gains the segment that the other loses.
cards.text: Misaligned homologues can produce a duplication and a reciprocal deletion through {{c1::unequal crossing over}}.
cards.question: Misaligned homologues can produce a duplication and a reciprocal deletion through {{c1::unequal crossing over}}.

cards.explanation: Read along the chromosome and locate the second copy relative to the first.
cards.text: If ABCDEF becomes ABCDCDEF, the extra CD immediately beside the original is a {{c1::tandem duplication}}.
cards.question: If ABCDEF becomes ABCDCDEF, the extra CD immediately beside the original is a {{c1::tandem duplication}}.

cards.explanation: Its position distinguishes it from an immediately adjacent repeat.
cards.text: A duplicated segment inserted away from the original segment is a {{c1::displaced duplication}}.
cards.question: A duplicated segment inserted away from the original segment is a {{c1::displaced duplication}}.

cards.explanation: An extra copy can change how much product is made even when the coding sequence is intact.
cards.text: A duplication can affect development by altering gene {{c1::dosage}}.
cards.question: A duplication can affect development by altering gene {{c1::dosage}}.

cards.explanation: Divide three by two. Regulation can modify this simple prediction.
cards.text: If protein output scales with gene copy number, three copies would yield {{c1::1.5 times}} the output of two.
cards.question: If protein output scales with gene copy number, three copies would yield {{c1::1.5 times}} the output of two.

cards.explanation: The segment remains present in reverse order.
cards.text: If ABCDEF becomes ABEDCF, the rearrangement affecting CDE is an {{c1::inversion}}.
cards.question: If ABCDEF becomes ABEDCF, the rearrangement affecting CDE is an {{c1::inversion}}.

cards.explanation: A rearrangement can therefore alter phenotype even when copy number is unchanged.
cards.text: Moving an intact gene into a different regulatory neighbourhood can change its expression through a {{c1::position effect}}.
cards.question: Moving an intact gene into a different regulatory neighbourhood can change its expression through a {{c1::position effect}}.

cards.explanation: It spans the two arms. A paracentric inversion stays within one arm.
cards.text: An inversion that includes the centromere is {{c1::pericentric}}.
cards.question: An inversion that includes the centromere is {{c1::pericentric}}.

cards.explanation: The centromere lies outside the inverted segment.
cards.text: A paracentric inversion is confined to {{c1::one chromosome arm}}.
cards.question: A paracentric inversion is confined to {{c1::one chromosome arm}}.

cards.explanation: A balanced carrier can have no net gain or loss of material and still produce unbalanced gametes.
cards.text: An exchange of segments between nonhomologous chromosomes is a reciprocal {{c1::translocation}}.
cards.question: An exchange of segments between nonhomologous chromosomes is a reciprocal {{c1::translocation}}.

cards.explanation: The term describes dosage. A breakpoint can still disrupt a functional sequence.
cards.text: A translocation with no appreciable net gain or loss of DNA is described as {{c1::balanced}}.
cards.question: A translocation with no appreciable net gain or loss of DNA is described as {{c1::balanced}}.

cards.explanation: A child may inherit an unequal set of segments from a balanced carrier.
cards.text: An unbalanced translocation can produce a partial deletion together with a partial {{c1::duplication}}.
cards.question: An unbalanced translocation can produce a partial deletion together with a partial {{c1::duplication}}.

cards.explanation: A common rearrangement brings MYC on chromosome 8 near an immunoglobulin regulatory region.
cards.text: The characteristic translocation in Burkitt lymphoma deregulates {{c1::MYC}} expression.
cards.question: The characteristic translocation in Burkitt lymphoma deregulates {{c1::MYC}} expression.

cards.explanation: Rearrangement can bring a growth-regulating gene under different transcriptional control.
cards.text: The chromosome carrying MYC before its characteristic rearrangement in Burkitt lymphoma is chromosome {{c1::8}}.
cards.question: The chromosome carrying MYC before its characteristic rearrangement in Burkitt lymphoma is chromosome {{c1::8}}.

cards.explanation: A translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 produces a constitutively active kinase associated with chronic myeloid leukaemia.
cards.text: The Philadelphia chromosome carries the {{c1::BCR–ABL1}} fusion gene.
cards.question: The Philadelphia chromosome carries the {{c1::BCR–ABL1}} fusion gene.

cards.explanation: The shortened derivative chromosome 22 is the Philadelphia chromosome.
cards.text: The two chromosomes involved in the characteristic CML translocation are {{c1::9 and 22}}.
cards.question: The two chromosomes involved in the characteristic CML translocation are {{c1::9 and 22}}.

cards.explanation: Their centromeres lie close to one end. Robertsonian fusions involve their long arms.
cards.text: The five human acrocentric autosomes are {{c1::13, 14, 15, 21 and 22}}.
cards.question: The five human acrocentric autosomes are {{c1::13, 14, 15, 21 and 22}}.

cards.explanation: A balanced carrier typically has 45 chromosomes because the fused long arms count as one.
cards.text: Fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes is a {{c1::Robertsonian translocation}}.
cards.question: Fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes is a {{c1::Robertsonian translocation}}.

cards.explanation: Two long arms are carried on a single derivative chromosome.
cards.text: A balanced carrier of a 13;14 Robertsonian translocation typically has {{c1::45}} chromosomes.
cards.question: A balanced carrier of a 13;14 Robertsonian translocation typically has {{c1::45}} chromosomes.

cards.explanation: The extra long arm can be attached to another chromosome, so total chromosome count alone can miss the diagnosis.
cards.text: A child with translocation Down syndrome has excess {{c1::chromosome 21q}} material.
cards.question: A child with translocation Down syndrome has excess {{c1::chromosome 21q}} material.

cards.explanation: A parental karyotype can identify a balanced carrier and inform recurrence counselling.
cards.text: In a 14;21 translocation, transmission of excess chromosome 21 long-arm material can cause {{c1::Down syndrome}}.
cards.question: In a 14;21 translocation, transmission of excess chromosome 21 long-arm material can cause {{c1::Down syndrome}}.

cards.explanation: The clinical effect depends partly on the tissues involved.
cards.text: Two or more genetically distinct cell populations derived from one zygote constitute {{c1::mosaicism}}.
cards.question: Two or more genetically distinct cell populations derived from one zygote constitute {{c1::mosaicism}}.

cards.explanation: A parent can transmit a variant even if it is undetectable in a blood sample.
cards.text: Mosaicism confined to cells that give rise to gametes is called {{c1::gonadal mosaicism}}.
cards.question: Mosaicism confined to cells that give rise to gametes is called {{c1::gonadal mosaicism}}.

cards.explanation: Chromosome-level changes can affect several genes and organ systems at once.
cards.text: Multiple congenital anomalies together with unexplained developmental difficulties can prompt {{c1::cytogenetic analysis}}.
cards.question: Multiple congenital anomalies together with unexplained developmental difficulties can prompt {{c1::cytogenetic analysis}}.
